title: Evening kindness
hookLine: one kind word before the day ends
tomorrow: can you really put a worry down, or does it follow you to bed?

lines: BE YE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.
cards: Sleep on it is good advice for a job offer or a big purchase. There's one thing an old letter says you must not sleep on.
In the New Testament's letter to the Ephesians, a writer who calls himself a prisoner says this: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Read it twice and it gets strange.
First, it seems to allow the anger. Be ye angry. Second, it sets a clock, and the clock is the sunset.
Why would a letter about holiness give anger permission, and then give it a deadline?

teach.h: GIVE NO PLACE: GRUDGES MOVE IN AT NIGHT.
teach.b: The next line solves half of it: Neither give place to the devil. In the letter, the feeling isn't the problem. Anger can flare in anyone who cares about something.
The problem is what anger does overnight. Kept past sundown, it settles in. It gets a room in the house, a place.
By morning it has furniture. So the sunset isn't a punishment; it's a door closing before the grudge moves in.

The other half comes a few lines later, and it's the cure: Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
And then: be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another.
The Greek word for kind there, chrestoi, can also mean useful, the way a good tool is useful. The clock stuck.
The Rule of Benedict, the guide for monks, lists among its tools of good works making peace with an adversary before the sun sets. Notice how small the ask is. Not a full resolution.
One word, kind and true, sent out before dark, so the night doesn't get the last say.

how: The Rule of Benedict counts making peace with an adversary before sunset among a monk's tools of good works, taking its clock from Ephesians 4:26.

o: a rule to keep quiet about anger until the morning
a polite goodnight text sent to everyone you know
a kind word sent out before the day is over

p: let not the sun go down

s: Ephesians says getting angry is always a sin
it says 'be ye angry, and sin not': the line is about what you do with anger, and how long you keep it.
the Rule of Benedict tells monks to make peace before the sun sets
it's on the list of the tools of good works.
the letter's cure for anger is going silent
it asks for words 'good to the use of edifying' and for kindness, not silence.

games.q: your sister mocked you at dinner and you're still angry at bedtime. what does the letter actually allow?
o: the anger, but not carrying it on into the night.
no anger at all: a kind person never feels it.
anger, as long as you never say it out loud.
games.why: 'Be ye angry, and sin not' gives the feeling room and then a clock: settle it, or at least soften it, before sundown.

practice: Bring to mind one person you were short with today, or one person who could use a kind word from you. Write them a single sentence, kind and true, with no explaining and no case for yourself.
Send it now, or keep it ready for the morning, and breathe out the rest.

wordCard.voice: Evening kindness: one kind word sent out before the day ends, so anger doesn't spend the night.

orig.note: Greek: kind, also useful or good. The word for 'kind' in Ephesians 4:32.

carryVoice: Pocket this: one kind word, sent out before the sun goes down on it. Good night.
